patients.summary: Management consultant in her late twenties with lifelong heavy periods and restrictive eating who develops iron deficiency anemia, then an acute porphyria attack, then post-infectious cold agglutinin hemolysis, then a right Bell's palsy, each after a cold or a lean stretch. Records arrive late or not at all for some outside care.

documents.title: New patient call
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Caller wants to transfer her care here; moved to the area last year and her old doctor is two hours east. Works as a consultant and travels a lot, prefers early-morning slots. Booked new patient visit 7/12 at 7:40. Asked her to sign the release so we can pull her old records. Membership paperwork emailed.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
26 y/o woman establishing care. Consultant, on the road 2-3 days most weeks, says she runs on coffee.

No active complaints today. Periods have always been heavy: first 2-3 days she changes a pad or tampon every 1-2 hrs, occasional small clots, 6-7 days total, regular. Cramps handled with ibuprofen 400 as needed.

Eating: often skips breakfast and lunch on client days, admits she keeps her intake tight on purpose because she wants to stay at her current weight. Few fruits or vegetables. Denies purging or laxative use. Gets several colds a year, all self-limited, no pneumonias or hospital stays.

PMH: as above. PSH: tonsillectomy at 8, wisdom teeth out at 22.
Meds: multivitamin w/ iron (takes maybe half the days), ibuprofen PRN.
Allergies: none to medications.
FH: mother with lupus. Father with hypertension. Maternal grandmother had acute intermittent porphyria. A paternal aunt had a Bell's palsy.
SH: single, lives alone. Never smoked. Has never drunk alcohol. No drug use.

Exam: thin, well-appearing. BP normal. HEENT normal, conjunctivae pink. Neck supple, no thyroid enlargement. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. Skin normal. Neuro grossly intact. Mood bright.

A/P
1. Heavy menstrual bleeding, longstanding. Ibuprofen with food.
2. Restrictive eating / meal skipping. Talked about regular meals and why it matters for energy. She heard me; will see.
3. Recurrent colds, nothing worrisome in the history.
4. HM: HIV and hep C screen today. Release signed for old records. Come back in the winter for a full physical with fasting labs.

PHQ-2 0.

documents.title: Your screening tests
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Hannah, both screening tests (HIV and hepatitis C) came back negative. Nothing else to do on those. Front desk will reach out to set up your physical for the winter. -PCP

reports.text: Outside report, prior primary care office. Specimen: cervical, liquid-based. Satisfactory for evaluation; endocervical/transformation zone component present.
reports.conclusion: Negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy.

documents.body: 38 pages received from patient's previous primary care office (2014-2022). Pertinent: Pap 6/2021 NILM. Tdap 3/2019. COVID Pfizer x2 spring 2021. HPV series completed as a teenager per immunization history. Tonsillectomy age 8. No hospitalizations. Problem list there: heavy menses, frequent URIs. Med list: MVI w/ iron, ibuprofen PRN. NKDA. Immunizations entered. Forwarded to PCP.

documents.title: Office Visit - Fatigue
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Came in because she is wiped out. Over about a month she has been more and more tired and gets woozy when she stands up quickly, worse on long client days. Periods unchanged, still very heavy. Still skipping meals most workdays. No black or bloody stools, no weight loss, no recent illness. No chest pain, no syncope.

Meds: MVI w/ iron off and on, ibuprofen for cramps.

O: Looks tired. Conjunctivae pale. Heart regular, soft systolic flow murmur at the left sternal border, no radiation. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft. No edema.
In-office CBC this morning: Hgb 8.2, MCV 72. Ferritin sent.

A/P: Microcytic anemia, almost certainly iron deficiency from years of heavy periods plus low intake. Murmur fits with the anemia.
- Ferrous sulfate 325 mg once daily, with food or OJ, not with coffee. Expect dark stools.
- Regular meals, iron-rich foods - she is willing to try a packed breakfast.
- Recheck CBC in ~8 wks.
- Return sooner for chest pain, fainting, shortness of breath.

Addendum 16:50: ferritin 5. Confirms iron deficiency. Plan unchanged.

documents.title: Iron level
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hannah - your ferritin (iron stores) came back at 5, which is very low and explains the tiredness. Keep the iron tablet going every day. It can take a few weeks before you feel a difference. We'll recheck your blood count in early June.

documents.title: RE: Iron level
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Thanks. Already picked it up last night. Can I take it at night instead? Mornings are chaos.

documents.title: RE: Iron level
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Nighttime is fine as long as you've eaten something.

documents.title: iron + coffee?
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Quick question, does it matter if I take the iron near my coffee? I drink a lot of it.

documents.title: RE: iron + coffee?
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Best to separate them by a couple of hours, coffee and tea cut down how much iron you absorb. Your evening dose plan works well for that.

documents.title: Follow-up - Iron deficiency anemia
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Taking ferrous sulfate most evenings, maybe misses 1-2 a week. Less tired, no more lightheadedness getting out of bed. Periods same. Eating breakfast more often, still skips lunch.

BP fine. Conjunctivae less pale. Still a faint flow murmur. Lungs clear.

CBC today: Hgb 10.6, up from 8.2.

A/P: IDA improving on oral iron. Continue. Recheck CBC and ferritin in the fall. Encouraged her to keep the lunch habit going.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, low MDM

documents.title: Follow-up - Anemia
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Feels like herself again, energy fine through long days. Has been on iron ~6 months. No lightheadedness. Periods unchanged.

Exam: well-appearing, conjunctivae pink. Heart regular, murmur no longer audible. Lungs clear.

Labs: Hgb 12.3, ferritin 34.

A/P
1. Iron deficiency anemia - resolved. Stop ferrous sulfate. Keep the MVI with iron daily (she admits it's still hit or miss). Heavy periods remain the driver; she'll let me know if fatigue comes back.
2. Flu and updated COVID given today.
RTC for physical in the spring.

documents.title: Blood count back to normal
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Your hemoglobin is 12.3 and iron stores are 34 - both back in the normal range. You can stop the iron tablets now. Try to keep up with the multivitamin.

conditions.label: Acute intermittent porphyria
conditions.note: acute attack after a cold, OTC cold medicine and restricted intake

procedures.procedure: Hospital discharge day management, 30 minutes or less

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary (outside, received)
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL - INTERNAL MEDICINE DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 02/01/2024 via the emergency department. Discharged 02/05/2024.
Allergies: NKDA.

Presentation: 27-year-old woman, management consultant, came to the ED after several days of on-and-off crampy abdominal pain and steady fatigue, with intermittent numb hands and feet and trouble focusing at work. No fever, vomiting, diarrhea or change in bowel pattern. She had a cold the prior week and took an over-the-counter multi-symptom cold product for several days. She has also been eating very little, by choice, to keep her weight down. Known heavy menses; iron deficiency anemia previously, treated by her PCP. Family history notable for a maternal grandmother with acute intermittent porphyria; mother with lupus; father hypertensive; paternal aunt with Bell's palsy. Never smoker, no alcohol.

ED exam: anxious-appearing, alert and oriented. Abdomen soft with mild tenderness on deep palpation, no rebound, no guarding. Diminished pinprick in a stocking-and-glove pattern; strength and reflexes preserved. Remainder of exam unremarkable.

Data: Na 131 (mildly low); rest of chemistry panel and CBC unremarkable. UA: dark amber, no evidence of infection, no blood. Spot urine porphobilinogen 42 mg/g creatinine (ref <2).

Hospital course: Acute attack of acute intermittent porphyria, likely precipitated by the cold remedy and prolonged caloric restriction. Started on IV 10% dextrose in the ED and admitted. Hematology consulted; IV hemin 3 mg/kg daily given for 4 days. Pain settled by day 2 without opioids; sodium improved with dextrose and normal intake. Tolerating regular meals by day 3. Numbness improving but not gone at discharge.

Discharge diagnoses: acute intermittent porphyria, acute attack; mild hyponatremia.
Discharge meds: unchanged (multivitamin with iron daily, ibuprofen 400 mg q6h PRN cramps - ibuprofen is considered safe in porphyria).
Instructions: do not fast or crash diet, eat regular carbohydrate-containing meals; check every new medication, including OTC products, against the porphyria drug-safety list provided; hematology follow-up in 4-6 weeks; PCP within 1 week; return for recurrent abdominal pain, weakness or confusion.

Scanned by MA 2/27/24 after records request of 2/9.

documents.title: I was in the hospital
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Hi, wanted to let you know I was admitted last week, Thursday through Monday. They said it was an acute porphyria attack (same thing my grandmother had). Bad stomach cramps and my hands and feet went numb. They gave me IV sugar and a medicine called hemin for 4 days. Feeling a lot better but still tingly. They told me to see you this week. I have a paper list of meds to avoid.

documents.title: RE: I was in the hospital
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Sorry to hear that, glad you are on the mend. Booked you Friday 2/9 at 8:00 with your PCP. Please bring the discharge paperwork and the medication list.

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Post-discharge visit, info from patient and her discharge instructions sheet (no summary from the hospital yet - requested today).

Hospitalized 2/1-2/5 with what was called an acute porphyria attack. Says it started with cramping belly pain and exhaustion a few days after a cold, for which she'd taken an OTC cold product, and she had been eating very little. Hands and feet went numb, couldn't concentrate. Got dextrose and 4 days of hemin. Cramps gone since the weekend. Still mild tingling in fingertips and toes, better each day. Thinking clearly again. Eating 3 meals a day since discharge.

Exam: well, a bit tired-looking. Abdomen soft, nontender. Pinprick slightly reduced in toes only; strength 5/5, reflexes 2+ and symmetric. Gait normal.

A/P
1. Acute intermittent porphyria, first recognized attack, recovering. Added to problem list. Reviewed the drug-safety list with her and scanned it to the chart; flagged in the allergy/alert section as a chart alert (not an allergy). Every new med, including OTC, gets checked first. No fasting. She will look into a medical alert bracelet.
2. Hyponatremia during admission - recheck BMP today.
3. Hematology follow-up being arranged by the hospital; she has the number.
RTC 3 months or sooner.

Addendum: BMP today normal, sodium back in range. Records request - hospital admission 2/1-2/5/2024.

documents.title: Records request follow-up
documents.author: MA
documents.body: No reply to 2/9 fax. Called hospital medical records - request was not in their queue. Re-faxed with patient's signed release. They quoted 5-7 business days.

documents.title: Records received - hospital admission
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Discharge summary for 2/1-2/5/24 stay arrived today, 18 days after our request (first fax went unanswered, called medical records on 2/20). Scanned and routed to PCP. ED physician note not included.

documents.title: Records review
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Reviewed hospital discharge summary. Urine PBG 42 mg/g Cr at presentation, Na 131. Matches her account. No changes.

documents.title: Hematology Consultation (outside, received)
documents.author: hematology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE HEMATOLOGY GROUP - CONSULTATION
Date of service: 03/07/2024
Reason: follow-up after inpatient treatment of acute porphyria attack

Ms. O'Brien is a 27-year-old woman whom we saw in the hospital in early February during her first recognized attack of acute intermittent porphyria (urine PBG 42 mg/g creatinine), treated with hemin x4 days and IV dextrose. Likely triggers: an OTC cold preparation and prolonged low calorie intake. Strong family history (maternal grandmother).

Today: no abdominal pain since discharge. Residual tingling of the toes is fading. Energy fair. Periods heavy, cycles regular.
Meds: multivitamin with iron, ibuprofen PRN. NKDA.
Exam: well. Abdomen benign. Distal sensation nearly normal; strength full.

Impression: acute intermittent porphyria, single acute attack, recovering.
Plan:
- No prophylactic therapy indicated after a single attack.
- Avoid fasting and porphyrinogenic drugs; review medications against the drug-safety database before starting anything new. Ibuprofen and acetaminophen acceptable.
- Consider a medical alert bracelet.
- Return as needed, or promptly for any symptoms of an attack.

cc: primary care physician

documents.title: cold medicine?
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Coworkers are all sick. If I catch it, what can I take? I'm scared to touch anything from the cold aisle now.

documents.title: RE: cold medicine?
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Good instinct to ask. Acetaminophen and ibuprofen are both fine for aches. Saline spray, fluids, honey and rest. Before any combination cold product, check it against the list or send me a picture of the label. And keep eating even if you don't feel like it.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
28 y/o here for a physical.

Interval: porphyria attack in Feb, treated inpatient; hematology saw her in March, no prophylaxis needed. Numbness in hands and feet is completely gone as of about April. No abdominal pain since. Eating three meals most days now - says the hospital stay scared her into it. Periods unchanged. Energy good. Still gets the occasional cold, nothing since winter.

Meds: MVI w/ iron (better about it lately), ibuprofen PRN.
NKDA. Chart alert: acute porphyria drug-safety list.
SH: unchanged. Never smoker, no alcohol.

ROS otherwise negative.

Exam: BP normal. Well-nourished, slim. HEENT normal, conjunctivae pink. Thyroid normal. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, no masses. Pelvic: normal external genitalia, cervix normal, Pap obtained. Extremities warm, no edema. Neuro: sensation intact to pinprick and vibration in hands and feet; reflexes symmetric. Skin normal.

PHQ-9: 2.

A/P
1. Health maintenance: Pap today. CBC, CMP, lipids, ferritin.
2. AIP - quiet since February. Neuropathy resolved.
3. Heavy menses / meal skipping - noted; regular meals encouraged.
Flu and COVID in the fall.

documents.title: Your physical labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Hannah - blood count, chemistries, cholesterol and iron stores all normal. Pap result will take about a week; I'll message you when it's in.

documents.title: Pap result
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Your Pap smear was normal. Next one due in 3 years.

documents.title: Fall vaccines
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Hi Hannah, flu and COVID vaccines are in. Reply with a morning that works and we'll set up a nurse visit.

documents.title: RE: Fall vaccines
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Tuesday 10/15 early if possible. Thanks!

documents.title: Nurse Visit - Vaccines
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Influenza (trivalent) 0.5 mL IM L deltoid and 2024-25 COVID (Pfizer) 0.3 mL IM R deltoid. Both on her porphyria safety list as acceptable - checked before giving. Tolerated, observed 15 min. VIS provided.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary (outside, received)
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL - MEDICINE SERVICE DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admission 02/02/2025 - Discharge 02/05/2025
Allergies: NKDA. Alert: acute intermittent porphyria - medications checked against porphyria safety database.

History: 28-year-old woman with lifelong menorrhagia, a pattern of restrictive eating, previously treated iron deficiency anemia and acute intermittent porphyria (one attack, 02/2024), admitted after 3 days of fatigue and dark urine. Dizzy on standing and mildly winded on stairs. The week before she had a mild cough and low-grade temperature that went away on its own. No abdominal pain, numbness or confusion.
PSH: tonsillectomy (age 8), third molar extraction (age 22).
FH: maternal grandmother AIP; mother SLE; father HTN; paternal aunt Bell's palsy.
SH: management consultant; never smoker; no alcohol.
Home meds: multivitamin with iron daily (irregular), ibuprofen 400 mg q6h PRN.

Exam on admission: BP 112/68, HR 98. Scleral icterus. Spleen tip palpable, mildly enlarged; no lymphadenopathy. Heart and lungs normal; abdomen otherwise benign. Neuro exam normal.

Data: Hgb 8.2 g/dL, MCV 90, reticulocytes 8%. Total bilirubin 3.2 (direct 0.4). LDH 486 U/L. Haptoglobin undetectable (<10). DAT positive for C3d, negative for IgG. UA: dark, no blood on dipstick, no RBCs. Urine PBG 1.1 mg/g Cr (normal) - not a porphyria attack.

Assessment: Cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia, complement-mediated, following a recent respiratory illness.

Course: Kept warm, warmed IV fluids. No transfusion needed; hemoglobin held steady through the stay. Folic acid started. Energy improving and urine lighter by discharge. Steroids not used (generally ineffective for this type).

Discharge meds: NEW folic acid 1 mg PO daily. Continue multivitamin with iron, ibuprofen PRN.
Instructions: dress warmly, avoid cold exposure and cold drinks; PCP visit within 1 week with CBC; hematology clinic in about 5-6 weeks; return for worsening fatigue, chest pain, breathlessness or very dark urine.

documents.title: Discharge summary received
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Discharge summary from regional hospital (2/2-2/5/25) came through on the fax this morning. Scanned. Pt needs a post-discharge visit within a week - called her, booked Tue 2/11 7:40.

documents.title: Post-Discharge Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Reviewed discharge summary (2/2-2/5). Admitted with fatigue and dark urine a week after a cough/low fever; found to have cold agglutinin-type autoimmune hemolysis (DAT C3d+, IgG-), Hgb 8.2, bili 3.2. Urine PBG normal, so not a porphyria flare.

Since home: still tired, less dizzy standing up. Urine back to normal color. Wearing gloves and a hat, which she never used to do. Taking folic acid daily. Working from home this week.

Exam: pale-ish, faint scleral icterus. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Spleen tip just palpable. No lymphadenopathy.

CBC today: Hgb 9.4 (up from 8.2).

A/P
1. Cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia, post-infectious, improving. Added to problem list; folic acid 1 mg added to our med list. Keep warm. Hematology appointment is set for mid-March. Repeat CBC in ~2 months if hematology doesn't send one.
2. AIP - no symptoms.
Call for worsening fatigue, SOB, or dark urine.

documents.title: Hematology appt
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Saw hematology yesterday. She was happy with how I'm doing and said my numbers are going the right way. Keep the folic acid, keep warm, see her again in a year or if anything changes. Not sure if they send you anything.

documents.title: RE: Hematology appt
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Good news. Nothing from them yet; we'll ask. Let's still do a blood count here in early April.

documents.title: Records request - hematology
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Faxed request to outside hematology for 3/13/25 visit note and labs.

documents.title: CBC result
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hgb 11.6, continuing to recover. Still nothing from hematology on the March visit. Message sent to pt.

documents.title: Blood count
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hemoglobin is 11.6 - nearly back to normal. Keep going with the folic acid. We'll check again at your physical in June.

documents.title: Refill - folic acid
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Pharmacy request: folic acid 1 mg #90. Originally from the hospital, now on our list. Approved by PCP x3 refills.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
29 y/o, physical.

Interval: hemolytic episode in Feb, recovering; hematology seen in March (no note received despite request). Feels well, energy normal, no dark urine. Still careful in the cold, kept gloves on through spring. No porphyria symptoms. Eating regular meals most days. Periods heavy as always, ibuprofen PRN.

Meds: folic acid 1 mg daily, MVI w/ iron, ibuprofen PRN. NKDA. Porphyria drug-safety alert on chart.

Exam: well-appearing. No scleral icterus. Conjunctivae pink. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, no organomegaly felt. No lymphadenopathy. Skin warm, normal. Neuro intact.
PHQ-9: 3.

A/P
1. Cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia - in remission clinically. Check CBC, bili today. Continue folic acid per hematology.
2. AIP - quiet.
3. HM: Pap up to date (2024). CMP, ferritin. Flu/COVID in the fall.

Addendum 6/18: Hgb 12.6, total bilirubin normal. Chemistries and ferritin normal. Portal message sent.

documents.title: Emergency Department Physician Note (outside, received)
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT - PHYSICIAN NOTE
Visit 02/12/2026

CC: right face drooping since this morning

HPI: 29-year-old woman with heavy menses, restrictive eating, past iron deficiency anemia, acute intermittent porphyria and cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and frequent colds. Noticed in the mirror this morning that the right side of her face would not move: cannot shut the right eye, cannot lift the right brow, smile pulls to the left. Just getting over a cold from a few days ago. No rash, no ear pain, no travel. No limb weakness, speech or swallowing trouble, or headache.
Meds: folic acid 1 mg daily, multivitamin with iron, ibuprofen PRN. NKDA.
FH: paternal aunt with Bell's palsy; maternal grandmother AIP.

Exam: Vitals unremarkable. Right face: no forehead wrinkling, eye does not close, flat nasolabial fold, mouth droops - complete upper and lower facial weakness. Ear canals and drums normal, no vesicles anywhere. Hearing grossly equal. Other cranial nerves intact. Strength, sensation, coordination and gait normal.

Impression: right Bell's palsy (idiopathic peripheral facial palsy).

Plan: prednisone 60 mg daily x7 days - checked against her porphyria drug-safety list, listed as safe. No antiviral given. Eye protection: lubricating drops every 2 hours while awake, tape the eye closed at bedtime, sunglasses outside. Follow up with PCP this week. Return for eye pain, vision change, new weakness, or trouble speaking or swallowing.

Dispo: home.

documents.title: Pt call - ED visit
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Pt calling, seen in ED yesterday for right-sided facial droop, told Bell's palsy. Started prednisone 60 daily and eye drops. Eye feels a little dry, no pain, vision fine. Taping it at night. Booked with PCP Tue 2/17 8:00. Advised to come in sooner or go back to ED for eye pain, vision change, or any arm/leg weakness. Asked her to bring ED paperwork; we'll request the note.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit - Bell's Palsy
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
ED follow-up. No ED note yet; working from her discharge sheet and her account.

Right facial weakness came on 2/12 a few days after a cold. ED diagnosed Bell's palsy, gave prednisone 60 mg x7 days (day 6 today) and eye lubricant. Face not changed since. Using drops faithfully, taping at night. No eye pain, no vision change. No ear pain, rash, hearing change. Eating OK.

Exam: Complete right facial weakness, forehead included; right eye does not fully close, Bell phenomenon present. Right cornea clear, no injection. No vesicles in ear or mouth. Other CNs intact. Limbs normal.

A/P: Right Bell's palsy, day 5.
- Finish prednisone. Checked: on her porphyria safe list.
- Eye care is the priority: keep drops, tape, glasses/sunglasses for wind.
- Expect gradual return over weeks to months. Video check in about 2 months, sooner for eye pain or redness.
- Requesting ED record.

documents.title: ED note received
documents.author: MA
documents.body: ED physician note from 2/12/26 visit received and scanned. Routed to PCP. PCP reviewed - consistent with visit of 2/17, no changes.

documents.title: face question
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Is it normal that nothing has changed yet? It's been almost 4 weeks. Eye is fine with the drops and tape.

documents.title: RE: face question
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Yes, that's within the usual range - recovery often starts around 3 to 6 weeks and then builds over months. Keep protecting the eye. If it's red or painful, let me know the same day. We'll do a video visit in April.

procedures.procedure: Telehealth visit, established patient, low MDM

documents.title: Video Visit - Bell's Palsy
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Video from her office, ID verified with DOB.

Right face has been coming back gradually since about mid-March. Can now close the right eye all the way, stopped taping about 2 wks ago, still uses drops occasionally on windy days. Forehead moves a bit. Smile still lopsided but better. No eye pain or redness.

On video: full right eye closure with effort and at rest blink. Some right brow elevation. Mouth corner lags on the right with smiling.

A/P: Bell's palsy, recovering well. Drops as needed. In person at her physical this summer.

documents.title: Refill - folic acid
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Refill request folic acid 1 mg #90 from pt's pharmacy. Physical booked 8/3. Approved x1 per PCP to carry her to that visit.

documents.title: Reminder
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Reminder call for physical 8/3 7:40. Pt confirmed.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
30 y/o for her physical.

Interval: right Bell's palsy in Feb, treated with prednisone in the ED; steady recovery since spring. She notices only a slightly uneven smile in photos. Eye fine, no longer needs drops. No porphyria symptoms; no dark urine or hemolysis symptoms; keeps warm in winter. Energy good. Eating meals regularly most weeks. Periods unchanged.

Meds: folic acid 1 mg daily, MVI w/ iron, ibuprofen PRN. NKDA. Porphyria drug-safety alert on chart.
SH: still consulting, traveling less. Never smoker, no alcohol.

Exam: well. Face: full forehead movement and complete eye closure on the right; slight lag of the right mouth corner only on a broad smile. Conjunctivae pink, no icterus. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. No lymphadenopathy. Neuro otherwise intact.
PHQ-9: 2.

A/P
1. Bell's palsy - near-complete recovery.
2. Cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia, in remission - CBC today; folic acid continued.
3. AIP - quiet; drug-safety alert in place.
4. HM: Pap due 2027. Flu/COVID this fall. CBC, CMP and ferritin today.
RTC in the fall.

documents.title: Physical labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Blood count, chemistries and iron stores look good. No changes - keep the folic acid going. See you in the fall.

documents.title: RE: Physical labs
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Great, thank you!

documents.title: Fall appointment
documents.author: patient
documents.body: You said fall - is late September ok? I can do 9/22 early.

documents.title: RE: Fall appointment
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Booked 9/22 at 7:40 with your PCP. Flu shot can be given then too if they're in.
